en.title: 7 Translated Horror Novels That Prove Fear Knows No Borders
en.summary: From cosmic car cults in Bolivia to demonic rock stars, discover seven recent international horror novels that are redefining terror. Explore how translated works offer fresh perspectives on universal fears.
en.body:
Horror transcends language, but the way it’s expressed can unlock startling new depths. As readers, we often gravitate towards the familiar, yet stepping outside our linguistic comfort zone can reveal chilling new landscapes of terror. Recent translations are doing just that, offering a global buffet of frights that speak to our deepest anxieties, proving that a good scare is truly a universal language.

## A World of Terrors Awaits

This year’s surge in translated horror fiction is a testament to the genre’s boundless creativity. We’re seeing everything from mind-bending cosmic dread to deeply personal psychological chills, all filtered through unique cultural lenses. Take **Maximiliano Barrientos’s** **Thousands of Eyes**, expertly translated by **Thomas Bunstead**. Set in Bolivia, this novel plunges readers into a disorienting world where speed-worshipping car cults clash with cosmic entities. Imagine spark plugs growing on trees and ritual sacrifices involving jumper cables or crashing into celestial trees. It’s a visceral, genre-bending experience that uses grief and trauma as fertile ground for otherworldly horror, all underscored by the roar of engines and the blast of black metal.

Then there’s **Rita Indiana’s** **Asmodeus**, brought into English by **Achy Obejas**. This work features a demon growing weary of inhabiting a decaying rock star. Seeking a vacation from the monotony, the demon embarks on a terrifying journey through a series of hosts, each encounter a descent into darker, more complex forms of horror. These novels, among others, demonstrate how translation doesn't just bring stories across borders; it brings new ways of feeling and fearing.

## Why This Matters to Global Fans

For avid readers and curious newcomers alike, the rise of translated horror is an invitation to expand their literary horizons. It’s about more than just discovering new authors; it’s about engaging with different cultural perspectives on fear, mortality, and the uncanny. These books challenge our assumptions and introduce us to narrative structures and thematic concerns we might not otherwise encounter. The sheer variety on display—from the surreal, car-obsessed cults of **Thousands of Eyes** to the demonic escapades in **Asmodeus**—highlights the rich tapestry of global storytelling. It’s a chance to connect with a worldwide community of horror enthusiasts who appreciate the craft and the creeping dread, regardless of the original language.

## What's Next

As more international horror finds its way into English, keep an eye on prominent literary translators and publishers specializing in global fiction. The landscape of horror is constantly evolving, and these translated works are at the forefront, offering fresh, vital voices that promise to keep us up at night.

Every culture on Earth has their own tales of terror, each the language used can reveal new nuances and complexities in the work, allowing readers to step outside their comfort zone in ways they never imagined. To show you what we mean, here are seven recent books that demonstrate the vast range and endless possibilities of horror in translation. Thousands of Eyes by Maximiliano Barrientos, translated by Thomas Bunstead A disorienting tale of cosmic horror and really cool cars, Thousands of Eyes puts you in the passenger seat with three separate narrators as they tell of their roles fighting a speed-worshipping car cult in Bolivia from the 1970s to the post-apocalyptic future. In the process, Barrientos outlines a twisted world where spark plugs grow on trees, brains are kept alive, a in jars, and ritual sacrifices involve either jumper cables or crashing full-speed into gigantic celestial trees. At the heart of the novel is a story of grief, trauma, and a thousand-eyed ghost fish that uses wounds both physical and spiritual to incubate itself, all backed by a soundtrack of engine roars and black metal albums. Asmodeus by Rita Indiana, translated by Achy Obejas Asmodeus, a demon inhabiting an aging rock star named Rudy, finds his host’s body more and more decrepit. Needing a break from all the monotony, he decides to take a vacation. His personal “safety route” out of Rudy involves rocketing through a series of bodies, including the occultist daughter of a torturer, a queer goth woman, metalheads, criminals, and other subterranean dwellers starting to emerge in the aftermath of a brutal dictatorship. Indiana deftly handles Asmodeus’ wild pinball ride through various subcultures with the acerbic humor and gift for visual poetry that made Tentacle such an absolute delight, and while Asmodeus is darker, it’s a unique and riotous take on demonic possession (each human is configured differently, with one being described as a “waiting room”), power dynamics, and the lingering scars left after experiencing horrors. Don’t Leave Her Alone by Desirée de Fez, translated by Lizzie Davis Spanish author Desirée de Fez weaves three strands of narrative between a mother and her two daughters, each carrying a number of personal issues and secrets that will lead to unnerving and gory events on Christmas Eve. As the clock ticks down to the bloody climax, we’re given horrifying insight into the lives of the desperate-for-normalcy Diana, the codependent Alba, and their mother Carmen.
